Joe Graham is in Kingsman.

Another very good student. In fact, he has an answer to my book on the corrido, a book on the conjunto, Manuel Peña, we just hired him. Yes, he was in Fresno, we had been trying to get him for a long time.

Pardon?
Did he start this semester?
He started this semester.
Mexican-American studies and Anthropology. Of course, he got his degree in Anthropology but his dissertation became a book, The Texas-Mexican Conjunto.

Even though the physical anthropologist tried to steal me away, my heart has always been and is today and always will be in folklore. All of the work-- What little fama I've made and name for myself, and the things that I've done and continued to do, are always in folklore.

children.text: Dr. Paredes, you were talking about los Vidales. My mother's a Vidal.
Yes?
Yes, my grandfather se llamaba Bernardo Vidal y Refugia Vidal. My mother was born in 1921, she's still alive. My mother has three sons, Bernardo, Lupe, and Librado Vidal. I lived in Coolidge Street.
Guadalupe Vidal there's an old name in the family-- Now, I am not familiar-- You see, your mother's generation is much younger than mine.
They came from Mexico.
You know very much about your grandparents, your great grandparents?
Not their great grandparents, no. I just know that my, Vidal, Bernardo Vidal, real tall, and--
Would you mind take his picture in his study?
Yes, ma'am, sure. [laughs]. [crosstalk] We will.
My mother just talks about his father a little bit, not as much. But now that Dr. Medrano is doing that, it's getting me more interested in it.
Her father is named Lupe?
No, her father was named Bernardo Vidal, Bernardo.
Yes, but probably he would've been about my age, or a little older.
No, my mother is 72, she was born 1921. So my grandfather would've been over a 100 by now, I would imagine, and so on.

Where did she live? The Vidales I'm talking about are probably the same people. The old man who was my mother's grandfather was named José María Vidal and he was the one that came from Spain. Either that, or his parents were newly arrived when he came here.

That was way back during colonial time, but he had a number of-- The sons he had, one was named Alberto Vidal. I knew him, I got to know him. He was tía Pilar's husband because the Vidales' and the Paredes' intermarried about the same time. In fact, on two levels, so I had first cousins
who were also my mother's first cousin. [laughter]

No, no intermixing, it's just that my tía Pilar, who was my father's sister, married Alberto Vidal, who was one generation above my mothers. Meanwhile, my mother married my father so you can see you have two Paredes' of the same generation marrying one Vidal here and one Vidal below. [chuckles]

The children of Alberto Vidal Paredes were my mother's first cousins because her mother and Alberto Vidal were brothers and they were my first cousins because their mother and my father were brother and sister. [laughs]
Dr. Paredes, you were in Brownsville when Narciso Martinez used to play? What are your recollections of Narciso Martinez?
The last thing-- Can I tell him? [laughter]

The last thing I remember about Narciso was the time that he spent the night here and we have gone away from the old border tradition of drinking coffee so strong that, according to the old legend, they would throw a horseshoe in it and if it didn't sink the coffee was not-- [laughter]

We drank a very weak coffee and decaffeinated. So Narciso, he and Nacho Montelongo, another singer who also is dead, they spent the night here. They were having breakfast and Narciso serves-- Of course, he was a pretty old man by then,

No se dio cuenta que estaba hablando, "Esto no es café, es agua". [laughter]
[Translation: He didn't notice he was talking, "This isn't coffee, it's water."]

Yo dije, "Narciso, te hacemos mejor café". He was very much embarrassed, [laughs] he said, "No, está bien". He drank the hot water. [laughter]
[Translation: I told him, "Narciso, we'll make you better coffee." He was very much embarrassed, [laughs] he said, "No, it's alright".]

It was hot water as far as he was concerned. [laughs] I knew him pretty well, when I was in Brownsville. Of course, he was a few years older than I and he was already playing at Las Prietas ¿Cómo se llama Las Prietas ahora? They changed the name, something gardens.
Garden park.
Garden park, what a name. [laughter] What's wrong with Las Prietas? Tenemos muchas prietas. [laughter] [Translation: We have many dark-skinned girls.]

En Las Prieta, en La Paloma, yo creo que La Paloma todavía se llama La Paloma. El Ranchito.
[Translation: In Las Prietas, in La Paloma, I think La Paloma is still called La Paloma. The little ranch.]

El Ranchito, en todos esos lugares tocaba él, tocaba Chicho. Chicho le decíamos nosotros, y seguimos- Yo lo fui a entrevistar varias veces y a platicar con él, fui a el- Vivia, ya no recuerdo, pero estaba cerca de San Benito.
[Translation: The little ranch, in all those places he played, Chicho did. Chicho is what we called him, and we - I went to interview him many times and to talk with him, I went to- He lived, I don't remember anymore, but it was close to San Benito.]
Sí, en La Paloma.

Era La Paloma, y lo trajimos a Austin más de una vez. Había una señora, Aida Barrera, que por un tiempo tuvo muy buenos grants y hizo una serie, de programas por radio, ¿cómo se llamaba? ¿Canciones algo? No me puedo acordar cómo se llamaba, and I was the host of it.
[Translation: It was La Paloma, and we brought him to Austin more than once. There was a woman, Aida Barrera, that for some time had really good grants and did a series of radio programs, what was it called? Songs something? I can't remember what it was called, and I was the host of it.]

We would bring somebody, Lydia Mendoza, for example. And Chicho, we had him here. I learned, I talked to him a good bit about this controversy of where we got the accordion, where we got the Polka. We did not get it from the Texas Germans.

The polka came to us from Paris to Mexico up to Monterrey, y le pregunté, "If you see something in print you get to believe it." ¿Cómo se llamaba este muchacho? [What was that man's name?] Chris Strachwitz. He did a wonderful job of collecting things but he was misled.

He was the one that sat down and print that Mexicans had got the-- The German Texans had brought the Hohner accordion and the polka. Le pregunto a Chicho y me dice, "Pues sí", le digo, "¿Bueno, te acuerdas de tu primer acordeón?" . "Sí", me dice. "Era una de, nada más una hilera de botones y era francesa".
[Translation: I asked Chicho and he says to me, "Well, yes", and I tell him "Well, do you remember your first accordion?". "Yes", he says. "It was one of, nothing more than a row of buttons and it was french".]

The French were the ones that-- Anyway, you know the Germans invented the accordion but they called it hand harmonica. It was the French who gave it the name accordion and popularized it before the Hohner people started bringing-- The polka again, polka begins Czechoslovakia,
the French pick it up and they're the ones that spread it from Paraguay all the way to the northwestern of United States.

We spoke with him one time, we interviewed one time, he told us that the first accordion he got was el Valentín for 12 pesos, en pagos [in installments]. [laughs] and he was very interesting, very knowledgeable.

Sí, Enrique Valentín tenía una mueblería obviamente, pero vendía fonógrafos también, victrolas como les decíamos porque eran de Victor y decían, "Victrola" on it. Eran de manija, the crank, eran las únicas que habían en ese tiempo. Él se interesó por un tiempo de llevar gente. Sí, Chicho fue--
[Translation: Yes, Enrique Valentín had a furntiture store obviously, but he sold phonographs too, Victrolas like we called them because they were from Victor and said 'Victrola' on them. They were hand-cranked, those were the only ones there were at that time. He got interested in taking people for some time. Yes, Chicho was--]

Hay gente que divide el crédito ese entre Chicho y el Flaco Jiménez original, Don Santiago Jiménez, de los primeros que popularizaron la polka pero el estilo de Chicho fue el que dominó por mucho tiempo. 
[Translation: There are people that divide the credit between Chicho and the original Flaco Jiménez, Don Santiago Jiménez, of the first who popularized the polka but Chicho's style dominated for a long time.]
You might check some of that on Manuel Peña's book, The Texas-Mexican Conjunto.

Sure. It's a mess- [video cut]
